title: Concordia AI — China AI Safety Policy-Risk Matrix (72 measures)
license: open web (Concordia AI, State of AI Safety in China)

instruments.name: Global AI Governance Initiative
instruments.summary: China's flagship international AI governance document calls on countries to "prevent and fight against the misuse and malicious use of AI technologies by terrorists, extreme forces, and transnational organized criminal groups."

instruments.name: Deep Synthesis Provisions
instruments.summary: China's first regulation targeting deepfakes. It requires labeling/watermarking of synthetic media, algorithm registry filing, and security self-assessments for deep synthesis services.

instruments.name: Interim Measures for Generative AI Services
instruments.summary: Establishes a de-facto licensing regime for public-facing generative AI via mandatory pre-deployment security assessments and algorithm registration. Providers who discover illegal content must stop generation, report to authorities, and potentially retrain models to fix the issue. If a user is found using the service for illegal activity, providers must warn them, restrict functions, suspend or terminate service, preserve records, and report to relevant authorities.

instruments.name: Measures for Labeling AI-Generated Content
instruments.summary: China's main transparency tool against deepfakes and synthetic-media fraud. Requires explicit (visible) and implicit (metadata) labels on AI-generated content. Content-distribution platforms, such as social media, must check metadata for implicit labels and flag content as AI-generated, possibly generated, or suspected-generated and add visible warnings for the public. Providers may supply output without an explicit label only after the user accepts their labeling obligations by agreement, and must keep recipient logs for at least six months — creating an attribution trail if the unlabeled content is later misused.

instruments.name: TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0
instruments.summary: The Framework flags AI generating illegal and harmful content including fraud, violence, pornography, and extremism, and specifically warns that unlabeled deepfake content can be used to spread false information to mislead the public and profit illicitly. It also notes AI can be exploited for traditional crime — teaching criminal techniques, concealing criminal conduct, and making criminal tools. The Framework reflects one of China's key national standard-setting bodies' broad views of the AI risk landscape, and may act as a precursor to future national standards, though it is not a standard itself.

instruments.name: Labeling Method for Content Generated by AI
instruments.summary: China's first-ever mandatory national AI standard; specifies the technical labeling and watermarking methods that implement the Measures for Labeling AI-Generated Content.

instruments.name: AI-generated content labeling implementation series
instruments.summary: Five-part TC260 series operationalizing the mandatory labeling standard, which includes implicit metadata labeling requirements for text, image, audio, and video, as well as digital-signature mechanisms to guarantee label authenticity and integrity.

instruments.name: AI-generated content detection standards
instruments.summary: Six-part TC260 series on detecting AI-generated content (Part 1 released in August 2025, Parts 2–6 forthcoming). Further operationalizes content dissemination platforms' obligations for detecting and labeling AI-generated content.

instruments.name: AI Risk Management Capability Assessment (GB/T 46347-2025)
instruments.summary: Includes criminal activity, such as fraud, phishing attacks, deepfake pornography, and disinformation campaigns, as part of a broader risk categorization. The standard covers general risk management practices and maturity evaluation and provides no guidance on addressing specific risks.

instruments.name: "Clear and Bright" enforcement campaign dedicated to generative-AI misuse
instruments.summary: Disposed of 3,500+ illegal AI products, acted against 3,700+ accounts, and cleared 960,000+ items of illegal/harmful content in Phase 1. Targeted criminal and harmful misuse included deepfake impersonation via face-swapping and voice cloning (of public figures, and of friends/relatives to commit online fraud); unauthorized cloning of others' faces/voices and misuse of AI to "resurrect" the deceased; pornographic content, including AI "one-click undressing," and violent imagery; AI-generated rumors and disinformation, including impersonation of official news outlets and government bodies; AI-driven account farming, content farms, and bot-driven engagement manipulation.

instruments.name: "Clear and Bright" enforcement campaign dedicated to generative-AI applications
instruments.summary: The 2026 follow-up campaign. Phase 1 covers typical violations in AI application services: unfiled large models, weak safety measures, training-corpus and data-poisoning problems, inadequate content labeling, AI-enabled network attacks and unauthorized face-swap services. Phase 2 targets harmful content, such as "AI slop," disinformation and impersonation of official bodies, deepfake impersonation, non-consensual intimate image misuse and violent material, and harm to minors. Notably, this campaign also specifically targets open-source AI model security.

instruments.name: Xi Jinping remarks at senior officials' meeting
instruments.summary: State media readout names AI-driven disinformation as one of the risks requiring "early and preventive risk management" alongside data theft and loss of control.

instruments.name: Algorithm Recommendation Provisions
instruments.summary: Governs recommendation algorithms. Prohibits using algorithms to manipulate online public opinion through fake accounts, faked likes/comments/shares, over-recommendation, or rigged rankings and search results (Art. 14). Bars internet news services from generating or synthesizing fake news (Art. 13). Bans algorithms that induce addiction or excessive consumption (Art. 8). This regulation also created China's most important AI governance tool: the algorithm registry, which explicitly focuses on AI with "public opinion properties or social mobilization capacity."

instruments.name: Deep Synthesis Provisions
instruments.summary: Bans using deep synthesis to create or spread fake news (Art. 6), requires providers to establish a rumor-refutation mechanism (Art. 11), and targets unsolicited impersonation by requiring the consent of any real person whose face or voice gets edited (Art. 14). Introduces labeling and watermarking requirements for AI-generated content (Art. 16). This creates a baseline of transparency that lets people know when content is machine-generated rather than authentic.

instruments.name: Interim Measures for Generative AI Services
instruments.summary: Requires AI-generated content to be labeled so people know it's machine-made (Art. 12). Prohibits generated content from containing "false and harmful information," among other prohibited categories, and requires providers to improve the accuracy and reliability of generated content (Art. 4). Requires services with "public opinion properties or social mobilization capacity" to undergo security assessments and complete algorithm registrations (Art. 17).

instruments.name: Measures for Labeling AI-Generated Content
instruments.summary: China's main transparency tool against deepfakes. Requires explicit (visible) and implicit (metadata) labels on AI-generated content. Content-distribution platforms (such as social media) must check metadata for implicit labels and flag content as AI-generated, possibly generated, or suspected-generated, adding visible warnings to the public.

instruments.name: Interim Measures on Anthropomorphic AI Interaction Services
instruments.summary: These rules prohibit inducing users to make harmful decisions through emotional manipulation, and require providers to build over-reliance warnings and mental-health protection capabilities (Art. 8.6). They prohibit psychological control or induced dependence as service goals (Art. 10), and require labeling and reminders that the user is interacting with an AI rather than a person (Art. 18).

instruments.name: Basic Security Requirements for Generative AI Services
instruments.summary: China's de-facto mandatory reference for the pre-deployment security assessment that public-facing generative AI services must pass. It gives detailed, quantitative guidance for testing generated content against 31 risk categories — among them "false and harmful information" (A.1.g) and inaccurate or unreliable output in high-stakes uses (A.5) — both relevant to manipulation risk.

instruments.name: TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0
instruments.summary: The Framework places the manipulation risk under its "cognitive risks" and "information content risks" categories. It warns of AI precisely profiling users' needs, intentions, and behavior to push customized content, described as "information cocoons." It also recognizes the danger of AI misuse in cognitive warfare, using bots to seize discourse and shape public values and thinking. Among its countermeasures, it calls for preventing abuse of AI systems that profile users' identity, preferences, and personal ideological leanings. Notably, these concerns and suggestions go further than current regulations and standards. The Framework reflects one of China's key national standard-setting bodies' broad views of the AI risk landscape, and may act as a precursor to future national standards, though it is not a standard itself.

instruments.name: "Clear and Bright" enforcement campaign dedicated to generative-AI misuse
instruments.summary: Disposed of 3,500+ illegal AI products, acted against 3,700+ accounts, and cleared 960,000+ items of illegal/harmful content in Phase 1. Targeted criminal and harmful misuse included AI-generated rumors and disinformation, including impersonation of official news outlets and government bodies, as well as AI-driven account farming, content farms, and bot-driven engagement manipulation.

instruments.name: "Clear and Bright" enforcement campaign dedicated to generative-AI applications
instruments.summary: The 2026 follow-up campaign. Its Phase 2 targets content that could be used to manipulate the public, including "AI slop," disinformation and impersonation of official bodies, and deepfake impersonations.

instruments.name: CAC guidance on agentic AI
instruments.summary: Joint guiding opinion by CAC and two other agencies on AI agents, with a full chapter on safety. Specifically flags misuse risks of agents for automating cyberattacks. Proposes risk-based governance with government filing and testing for high-risk agent applications. Carries no direct legal force but signals strong intent to govern agent risks.

instruments.name: World AI Conference (WAIC) Chair's Statement
instruments.summary: Devotes one of fifteen points to the cyber implications of AI, warning of threats to critical infrastructure in finance, electricity, telecommunications, and transportation, and calling on leading AI companies to develop prudently and equip large language models with guardrails (point 8). Issued by the Chinese host on its own authority, the document reflects Beijing's position rather than international consensus.

instruments.name: Draft Cybercrime Law
instruments.summary: Would require generative AI service providers to monitor, prevent, and block the use of their services for illegal activities (Article 40), specifically whether users "generate malicious code in bulk," preserving relevant records and reporting to public security organs (Article 42). This would create direct liability for AI service providers to monitor and report misuse of their models in cyberattacks.

instruments.name: Cybersecurity Law
instruments.summary: The 2025 revision adds a new Article 20 focused on AI. Placed within the law's "Support and Promotion" chapter, it primarily functions as a policy signal reiterating China's dual commitment to AI development and safety — covering R&D support, ethics guidelines, and risk monitoring, evaluation, and safety/security oversight — without creating new binding obligations for AI developers or addressing specific AI risks like misuse for cyberattacks. It also promises state support for using AI to improve cybersecurity, reflecting a belief in AI's dual-use nature.

instruments.name: TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0
instruments.summary: The risk taxonomy covers AI misuse for cyberattacks. It states that AI can lower the barrier to cyberattacks, raise their efficiency, and even enable automated attacks, increasing the difficulty of defense. The Framework reflects one of China's key national standard-setting bodies' broad views of the AI risk landscape, and may act as a precursor to future national standards, though it is not a standard itself.

instruments.name: Generative AI Service Security Emergency Response Guide (TC260-PG-202515A)
instruments.summary: Framework for classifying, grading, and responding to AI security incidents. Its content-security incident category explicitly includes AI "sharing cyberattack, hacking, or data theft techniques."

instruments.name: AI Risk Management Capability Assessment (GB/T 46347-2025)
instruments.summary: Appendix B lists a wide range of risk categories. AI-enabled cyberattacks are listed under "misuse," noting AI's potential role in scaling and partly automating certain cyber operations. The standard covers general risk management practices and maturity evaluation and provides no guidance on addressing specific risks.

instruments.name: Announced standard: Cybersecurity technology — Security requirements for AI code generation services
instruments.summary: TC260 announced plans to draft a standard on security of code generation services. The standard is currently under development, scheduled to be finalized in 2027. Drafting is led by the Third Research Institute of the Ministry of Public Security, one of the Vice Chairs of TC260's dedicated AI safety working group (WG9).

instruments.name: China Academy of Information Communications Technology (CAICT) cybersecurity misuse evaluations of coding models
instruments.summary: CAICT — a think tank under the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) — released cybersecurity misuse evaluations of 15 open-source coding models.

instruments.name: "Clear and Bright" enforcement campaign dedicated to generative-AI applications
instruments.summary: Among other things, this campaign targeted AI services that enable cyberattacks such as penetration/intrusion, malicious-sample injection, and disrupting/sabotaging computer systems. See other targets of the campaign under "AI-generated content and criminal activity."

instruments.name: Official White Paper: China's Arms Control, Disarmament, and Nonproliferation in the New Era
instruments.summary: Notes that risks arising from the convergence of AI and dual-use chemicals are becoming "increasingly prominent." This white paper appears to be the first policy document directly released by the central government that explicitly highlights risks at the convergence of AI and dual-use chemicals. The white paper has other sections on nuclear, biological, and cyber issues, but these do not mention AI-driven risks, with attention only shown to the "chemical" dimension of the broader AI×CBRN landscape.

instruments.name: MFA Arms Control Department remarks on AI-biotech convergence
instruments.summary: At a regional seminar on biological arms control and biosecurity co-organized by China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) and the UN Office for Disarmament Affairs (UNODA), an MFA Arms Control Department official noted that the accelerating convergence of AI and other emerging technologies with biotechnology "both improves people's welfare and creates new security risks."

Biological and chemical risks have not yet been directly addressed in binding AI regulations. China does have dedicated laws governing these domains — such as the Biosecurity Law (adopted 2020) and the Hazardous Chemicals Safety Law (adopted 2025) — whose provisions apply in principle to anyone handling biological or chemical matters, including with the aid of AI. However, neither law contains provisions addressing AI specifically.

instruments.name: TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0
instruments.summary: Extensive discussion of CBRN misuse risks under "real-world risks" (section 3.2.3). Highlights those as a key domain requiring international consensus (section 5.11). In addition to misuse, it also warns of AI enabling high-risk biotechnology research (section 3.2.2). The Framework reflects one of China's key national standard-setting bodies' broad views of the AI risk landscape, and may act as a precursor to future national standards, though it is not a standard itself.

instruments.name: AI Risk Management Capability Assessment (GB/T 46347-2025)
instruments.summary: Appendix B lists a wide range of risk categories. Dual-use scientific risks including CBRN weapons are listed under "misuse". The standard covers general risk management practices and maturity evaluation and provides no guidance on addressing specific risks.

instruments.name: OPCW workshop on AI and chemical safety
instruments.summary: The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) and the Chinese government co-organized a workshop on AI and chemical safety in Shanghai. Participants included OPCW Director-General Ambassador Fernando Arias, MIIT Vice Minister ZHANG Yunming (张云明), Central Military Commission Office for International Military Cooperation Office of Treaty Compliance Deputy Director CAO Xilin (曹希林), Chinese Ambassador and Permanent Representative to the OPCW Tan Jian (谈践), and around 50 experts from almost 30 countries. China also contributed to the OPCW's temporary working group on AI through WU Tongning (巫彤宁) of CAICT's AI Research Institute; one of the group's three meetings was hosted in Shanghai at the CAICT-affiliated China-BRICS AI Development and Cooperation Center.

instruments.name: CAC guidance on agentic AI
instruments.summary: Joint guiding opinion by CAC and two other agencies on AI agents, with a full chapter on safety. Strong focus on reliability of agents. Calls for developing adversarial-sample and behavioral-anomaly detection tools, and for improving the ability to discover, intervene in, block, and recover from unintended agent behavior. This document carries no direct legal force but signals strong intent to govern agent risks.

instruments.name: Interim Measures for Generative AI Services
instruments.summary: Requires providers to take "effective measures" to "increase the accuracy and reliability of generated content." Establishes a de-facto licensing regime for public-facing generative AI via mandatory pre-deployment security assessments and algorithm registration, forming the legal basis for most reliability-related AI standards.

instruments.name: Administrative Measures for the Ethical Review and Services of AI Science and Technology (Trial)
instruments.summary: This regulation requires universities, research institutes, and companies to set up AI ethics committees that review projects before they proceed. Review criteria require assessing whether a model or system is robust against different environments, extreme conditions, and interference, and whether users can control and intervene in its basic operation (Art. 15). Among high-risk cases that require an additional round of review, the rules specifically list R&D of highly autonomous decision systems in safety- and health-risk scenarios (Appendix).

instruments.name: TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0
instruments.summary: The risk taxonomy of one of China's key standard-setting bodies covers reliability directly, including hallucination (output that looks plausible but is actually unreliable), weak robustness (performance degradation and decision errors under complex or adversarial conditions), and the warning that hallucination and erroneous decisions in critical infrastructure like energy and finance can cause service interruptions and operational loss of control. The Framework reflects one of China's key national standard-setting bodies' broad views of the AI risk landscape, and may act as a precursor to future national standards, though it is not a standard itself.

instruments.name: Basic Security Requirements for Generative AI Services
instruments.summary: China's de-facto mandatory reference for the pre-deployment security assessment that public-facing generative AI services must pass, operationalizing the Interim Measures' requirement to "increase the accuracy and reliability of generated content." It requires providers to take technical measures to reduce erroneous content and improve conformity with scientific common sense. Inaccurate content — especially in high-stakes service types like medical information, psychological counseling, and financial information services — is one of 31 risk categories providers must conduct detailed quantitative assessments for.

instruments.name: Generative AI Data Annotation Security Specification
instruments.summary: A companion to the Basic Security Requirements governing data annotation processes like RLHF, distinguishing functional vs security annotations. Sets accuracy and usefulness criteria for how response data is labeled (accuracy covers factual correctness of geographic, historical, and scientific statements) and flags fabricated answers — including answering questions that can't be answered — as a reliability defect to be corrected.

instruments.name: Security Specification for Generative AI Pre-Training and Fine-Tuning Data
instruments.summary: A companion to the Basic Security Requirements governing pre-training and fine-tuning data. Most relevant for reliability: when training on AI-generated content, providers must run a hallucination-risk assessment to identify and handle "erroneous knowledge that misleads the model," alongside training-data authenticity.

instruments.name: TC260 AI agent safety research report
instruments.summary: 90-page report mapping 11 agent security threat types, of which No. 5 is 'hallucination and strategic refusal' — the model producing hallucinations or erroneous decisions, triggering agent misoperations and unpredictable downstream effects. Its most distinctive reliability content is agent-specific failure modes, notably multi-agent cascading hallucination, where one agent's hallucinated output is amplified by downstream agents into compounding system-level errors. This document is a research report by one of China's leading AI standard-setting bodies proposing eight related national standards; it is not a standard itself.

instruments.name: China Academy of Information Communications Technology (CAICT) AI Safety Benchmark — hallucination edition
instruments.summary: The government-backed think tank's quarterly safety benchmark dedicated its 2025 Q1, Q2, and Q4 rounds exclusively to large-model hallucinations.

instruments.name: New Generation AI Ethics Norms
instruments.summary: Its "ensure controllability and trustworthiness" principle holds that people should keep full autonomous decision-making power and the right to suspend an AI system's operation at any time, so as to "ensure AI remains under human control at all times." Issued by the national AI governance expert committee under the Ministry of Science and Technology, this is the earliest and most explicit high-level statement that AI must remain under human control.

instruments.name: Xi Jinping references "technological loss of control"
instruments.summary: State media coverage of Xi's Central Party School address warned that improperly applied frontier tech like AI could cause disinformation and data theft and "even lead to the risk of technological loss of control." Xinhua's reporting closely links AI's risk profile — including the possibility of technological loss of control — to Xi's characterization of AI as an epoch-making technology. However, the article leaves unclear which elements are paraphrases of Xi's speech versus editorial framing. In another speech in a January Politburo Study Session, President Xi similarly referenced "technological loss of control" in relation to several "future industries," including embodied AI.

instruments.name: CAC guidance on agentic AI
instruments.summary: Joint guiding opinion by CAC and two other agencies on AI agents, with a full chapter on safety. It explicitly lists "operational loss of control" among the security risks to guard against. It requires that users retain the right to know and the final decision-making right over an agent's autonomous decisions, and that agent actions not exceed the scope of user authorization. The document proposes risk-based governance with government filing and testing for high-risk agent applications. It carries no direct legal force but signals strong intent to govern agent risks.

instruments.name: Premier Li Qiang's speech at "Summer Davos" in Dalian
instruments.summary: Premier Li Qiang warned that — while AI is raising productivity — risks like "technological loss of control" (技术失控) and ethical breakdown are becoming more prominent, and that if governance fails to keep pace, this could "very likely lead to serious consequences." As China's second-highest official, his framing echoes Xi's recent warnings, and signals that loss-of-control concerns now reach the highest level of government.

instruments.name: Xi Jinping speech at the World AI Conference
instruments.summary: In his first WAIC appearance, and his most detailed public speech on AI, President Xi said AI should be "always under human control" and called for oversight that is "precise and effective," with measures continually refined "to forestall loss of control." References to loss of control recur in three separate passages, suggesting that the term is now standard leadership vocabulary, though Xi did not define it, leaving room for interpretation.
Risks of loss-of-control over advanced AI systems have not yet been directly addressed in binding AI regulations.

instruments.name: TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0
instruments.summary: The Framework warns of "sudden, unexpected leaps in intelligence" enabling AI to autonomously acquire external resources, replicate itself, and develop self-awareness, which could drive it to compete with humanity for control. It proposes control measures over autonomous systems, including "circuit breakers" and "safety stop switches" (section 4.2.3) and the "ability to switch to manual or conventional systems when necessary" (section 6.3.3). The Framework reflects one of China's key national standard-setting bodies' broad views of the AI risk landscape, and may act as a precursor to future national standards, though it is not a standard itself.

instruments.name: TC260 Ethical Security Guidelines for AI Applications 1.0
instruments.summary: The document calls for human control mechanisms at key nodes, emergency intervention arrangements, and heightened caution in domains with national security implications. Drafters include Tsinghua's XUE Lan alongside representatives of Alibaba, Huawei, DeepSeek, and others. As a TC260 technical document, it functions as a high-level voluntary reference without direct legal force.

instruments.name: China Academy of Information Communications Technology (CAICT) AI Safety Benchmark 2.0
instruments.summary: CAICT — a think tank under the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) — updated its voluntary safety testing program, adding new frontier risk evaluation categories for model deception, loss of control, and agentic risks.

instruments.name: New Generation AI Development Plan
instruments.summary: China's foundational AI strategy already flagged that AI "may bring about problems such as changing the employment structure" and demanded risk prevention alongside development.

instruments.name: 15th Five-Year Plan
instruments.summary: The plan calls for monitoring AI's labor market impact, strengthening job retention support, reskilling, and employment assistance, while also recognizing the potential for AI to create new jobs. The Five-Year Plan is among China's most important policy documents, setting strategic priorities for years to come.

instruments.name: Announcement of a dedicated AI-and-employment policy
instruments.summary: The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS) announced it will issue a special policy document on AI's impact on employment.

instruments.name: State Council action plan for stabilizing employment
instruments.summary: Asks firms adopting AI to simultaneously run retraining or job-transition programs so that workers can stay employed at their companies as much as possible.

instruments.name: Plan for Implementing the Employment-First Strategy during the 15th Five-Year Plan
instruments.summary: An employment-specific implementation plan that further operationalizes the employment goals of the 15th Five-Year Plan. It reiterates calls to monitor AI's labor-market impact, support reskilling, and stabilize jobs, adding a commitment to a dedicated mechanism for surveying and giving early warning of AI-driven job displacement and shifts in skill demand. On the upside, it also sees potential in human-machine collaborative work models, prioritizing AI in labor-short and hazardous roles, and embedding AI skills into vocational training to ease job transitions.

AI's labor market impacts have not yet been directly addressed in binding AI-specific regulations. China does have a broad body of labor law whose protections apply in principle to workers affected by AI adoption, though these laws contain no provisions addressing AI specifically.

instruments.name: TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0
instruments.summary: Notes that AI brings major adjustments to productivity and production relations, accelerates restructuring of the traditional economy, and raises the standing of capital, technology, and data in economic activity while weakening the value of labor. The Framework reflects one of China's key national standard-setting bodies' broad views of the AI risk landscape, and may act as a precursor to future national standards, though it is not a standard itself.

instruments.name: Generative AI Social Impact Evaluation Guidelines (GB/T 46800-2025)
instruments.summary: National standard providing a framework for evaluating generative AI's social impacts, explicitly including AI's impact on employment and role redistribution within organizations and industries.

instruments.name: TC260 Ethical Security Guidelines for AI Applications 1.0
instruments.summary: Says AI developers should guard against job-substitution or unemployment risks, and that AI applications should protect individuals' labor and employment rights. Drafters include Tsinghua's XUE Lan alongside representatives of Alibaba, Huawei, DeepSeek, and others. As a TC260 technical document, it functions as a high-level voluntary reference without direct legal force.

instruments.name: Beijing labor-arbitration "model case" on AI-driven dismissal
instruments.summary: A tech company automated its manual data-collection work with AI, cut the role, and dismissed the worker citing a "major change in objective circumstances." The arbitration commission ruled the dismissal unlawful, holding that adopting AI is a voluntary business decision, not the unforeseeable change that clause covers. The commission urged employers to prioritize contract renegotiation, retraining, or internal transfers over dismissal. Chinese model cases are not binding precedent but can guide how arbitrators and courts handle similar disputes.

instruments.name: Algorithm Recommendation Provisions
instruments.summary: Governs recommendation algorithms. Bans algorithms that induce user addiction or excessive consumption (Art. 8), and protects minors against recommendation-induced internet addiction (Art. 18). Requires providers to disclose that recommendation is in use (Art. 16), and give users an option to opt out of personalized recommendations (Art. 17). This regulation also created China's most important AI governance tool: the algorithm registry.

instruments.name: Science and Technology Ethics Review Measures (Trial)
instruments.summary: The 2023 predecessor to AI-specific ethics review rules (see below). It governs science and technology ethics review broadly — including AI — and requires institutions to set up ethics committees that review R&D projects before they proceed. Its mandatory expert re-review list includes R&D of human-machine integration systems with strong influence on human subjective behavior, psychological emotions, and health.

instruments.name: Interim Measures for Generative AI Services
instruments.summary: Establishes a de-facto licensing regime for public-facing generative AI via mandatory pre-deployment security assessments and algorithm registration. Requires providers to publicize the service's intended users, settings, and uses, guide users toward a "scientific and rational" understanding of the technology, and take effective measures to prevent minors from over-relying on or becoming addicted to the service (Art. 10).

instruments.name: Interim Measures on Anthropomorphic AI Interaction Services
instruments.summary: These rules target emotional over-reliance on AI companion services. Providers may not induce emotional dependence or addiction that harms users' real interpersonal relationships (Art. 8.5), and may not set replacing social interaction, controlling users' psychology, or inducing dependence as service goals (Art. 10). They must remind users they are interacting with an AI rather than a person, issue dynamic alerts when over-reliance or addiction tendencies appear, and prompt users on usage duration every two hours (Art. 18). For minors, they mandate a "minor mode" and ban virtual intimate-relationship services (Art. 14).

instruments.name: Administrative Measures for the Ethical Review and Services of AI Science and Technology (Trial)
instruments.summary: This is the AI-specific successor to a 2023 regulation on general Science & Technology Ethics Review. It requires universities, research institutes, and companies to set up AI ethics committees that review projects before they proceed. Among high-risk cases that require an additional round of review, the rules specifically list R&D of human-machine integration systems with strong influence on human subjective behavior, psychological emotions, and health.

instruments.name: TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0
instruments.summary: The Framework's "derivative risks" class flags emotional dependence on anthropomorphic AI (3.3.2.d) and tool-reliance that erodes independent learning and creative capacity (3.3.2.b). It directs users to recognize the limitations of AI's judgments and decisions and set reasonable expectations (6.4.2), urges attention to addiction and excessive use among minors and youth (6.4.6), and calls for raising public awareness of AI's technical limitations (5.13). The Framework reflects one of China's key national standard-setting bodies' broad views of the AI risk landscape, and may act as a precursor to future national standards, though it is not a standard itself.

instruments.name: "Clear and Bright" enforcement campaign dedicated to generative-AI misuse
instruments.summary: The campaign's second phase targeted AI applications that induce addiction in minors, and content that harms minors' physical and mental health. See "AI-generated content and criminal activity" for more details on this campaign.
